title: Intensity
summary:
Intensity refers to the perceived exertion during physical activity, and adjusting it is crucial for the safety of mother and fetus. It should be adapted each trimester, especially in the second and third, because of changes in balance and center of gravity.

Three methods are described: the Borg RPE scale, the speech test and heart rate (percentage of heart rate reserve, via the Karvonen formula). Combining them gives the most complete picture. Moderate activities are recommended, high intensity is to be avoided especially by inexperienced women, and advice differs for sedentary, active and athletic women.
points: The Borg RPE scale should be kept between 12 and 14, which corresponds to moderate effort, and remains useful when heart rate is affected by pregnancy.
The speech test: the woman should hold a conversation without difficulty; if out of breath to speak, intensity is too high.
The speech test is the most subjective of the three methods.
Moderate intensity corresponds to approximately 40-60% of heart rate reserve, generally aligned with RPE 12-14, calculated with the Karvonen formula.
Heart rate percentages should be recalculated at minimum each trimester, ideally monthly, or exceptionally weekly.
Moderate activities include walking, swimming, stationary cycling, prenatal yoga, Pilates and muscle strengthening; flexibility and relaxation are low intensity.
Sedentary women should start with gentle walking or water aerobics, keeping RPE between 12 and 13.
Active women can continue moderate activity such as gentle cycling, swimming or prenatal yoga at RPE 12-14.
Athletes could partially maintain high-intensity training adapted to pregnancy, while protecting uterine blood flow and preventing dehydration.
takeaways: Combine RPE, the speech test and heart rate monitoring for a comprehensive view.
Aim for RPE 12-14 (12-13 for sedentary women).
Use the talk test when no other tools are available.
Recalculate heart rate targets at least each trimester.
Choose moderate activities like walking, swimming, cycling or prenatal yoga.
Athletes should monitor heart rate and vital signs constantly.
cautions: High-intensity exercise should be avoided, especially by women with no prior experience, as it can increase risk of dizziness, fainting or decreased uterine blood flow.
Avoid exercises that risk abdominal trauma or falls.
Athletes must prevent dehydration and not compromise uterine blood flow.
